title_tag.en: A story of survival on Mars, built from real NASA data.

privacy.en: Use a nickname, not your real name. Saved only on this device. No account, no email.

rotate.en: Turn your phone sideways to play

m_air_g.en: Oxygen and water for the crew. Life Support makes it with power. If it reaches 0, the mission fails.

m_food_g.en: Food grown in the greenhouse. Plants need light (power) and water.

m_power_g.en: Units of electricity from the solar panels each sol. Dust makes the panels weaker.

m_shield_g.en: Radiation shield power. More shield means less radiation for the crew.

m_science_g.en: Discoveries your crew makes in the lab. It's why you came to Mars.

g_sol.en: A sol is one day on Mars: 24 hours and 39 minutes, a little longer than a day on Earth.

g_heat.en: A thick shell under the capsule. Air rubbing against it at huge speed makes it glow hot, and it protects everything inside.

g_delay.en: Radio travels at the speed of light, but Mars is so far away that a message takes 3 to 22 minutes, depending on where the planets are.

g_jezero.en: A crater on Mars that once held a lake, with an old river delta. NASA's Perseverance rover landed here in 2021.

g_eva.en: Extravehicular activity: going outside in a spacesuit. Outside, there are no walls to block radiation.

g_dustdevil.en: A spinning column of wind and dust. On Mars they can be taller than skyscrapers, and sometimes they blow dust off solar panels.

no_power.en: No free power left. Tap a room to unplug a cable first.

c1_sub.en: Jezero Crater, Mars · Your crew's first sols

c1_tagline.en: Land, wake the base, grow the first food.

c1_d1.en: Entering the Mars atmosphere at almost 20,000 km/h! The [[heat shield|heat]] is glowing hotter than lava.

c1_d2.en: Earth can't help us now. Our signal takes {min} minutes to reach them, so we land on our own. NASA calls this the 'seven minutes of terror'.

c1_d3.en: Engines... landing legs... hold on, Commander!

c1_l1.en: Touchdown! Welcome to [[Jezero Crater|jezero]], Commander {name}. Billions of years ago, this was a lake.

c1_l2.en: Where there was water, there might have been life. Finding out is our job.

c1_l3.en: But first things first. The base is still asleep. No power means no air, and the suits only last a few hours.

c1_l4.en: I'm NOVA, the base's AI. Our solar panels make 10 power units every [[sol]]. The rooms want more than that. You decide who gets power.

c1_obj_wake.en: Wake the base: share all 10 ⚡ between the rooms

c1_w1.en: Drag a glowing cable from the yellow ⚡ hub into a room. Each cable is 1 unit. Tap a room to take a cable back.

tip_ls.en: Life Support makes air and water. Four people breathe 14 air every sol, and each cable makes 7. So it needs at least 2.

tip_gh.en: The greenhouse grows food. The crew eats 10 food every sol, and each cable makes 6.

tip_lab.en: The lab is where discoveries happen. Each cable makes 4 science per sol.

tip_shield.en: The shield blocks radiation. Each cable stops 20% of it. Mars has a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field, so radiation is stronger here.

tip_comms.en: Comms keeps our link with Earth. Without it, nobody hears us and no warnings reach us.

w_need_all.en: Use all 10 cables. Power you don't use is wasted.

w_need_air.en: Air would run out! Life Support needs at least 2 cables.

w_need_food.en: Food would run out! The greenhouse needs at least 2 cables.

w_need_comms.en: Connect Comms, or Earth can't reach us.

c1_w_done.en: The base is alive! Did you notice? There wasn't enough power for every room. Real Mars missions face this every day.

c1_g1.en: Time to plant! Red romaine lettuce, the same kind astronauts grew and ate on the Space Station in 2015.

c1_g2.en: Plants need light and water. More light costs power, and water comes out of Life Support. Too much water and the roots can't breathe.

c1_g_great.en: Look at them! Big, healthy and red. That's a real harvest.

c1_g_ok.en: Not bad! A bit small, but it's food. Next time we can balance light and water better.

c1_g_bad.en: Hmm, they struggled. Plants are like us: they need the right amount, not the most.

c1_n1.en: Commander, bad news. Dust has settled on the solar panels. We're down to 8 power.

c1_n2.en: I could go out on an [[EVA|eva]] and brush them clean. But outside there are no walls between me and the radiation.

c1_c_eva_h.en: The panels are clean right away, but Deniz takes extra radiation and uses suit air.

c1_c_wait_h.en: Nobody goes outside, but the lab gets less power tonight. Wind might clean the panels... or not.

c1_eva_done.en: Panels clean! It's freezing out here, and my dose meter clicked a bit. Coming back in.

c1_wait_done.en: We're waiting. The lab is running on half power tonight.

c1_devil1.en: Wait... look outside! A [[dust devil|dustdevil]] is heading for the panels!

c1_devil2.en: It swept the dust right off! NASA's Spirit rover got lucky like this too. In February 2009, its power jumped from about 210 to 240 watt-hours in one day.

c1_end1.en: Sol 1 complete. We landed, the base is alive, and we have food growing. Not bad for a first day on Mars, Commander.

c1_end2.en: But I'm watching the horizon. The dust is getting thicker every day. Something big is coming.

c1_real.en: On February 18, 2021, NASA's Perseverance rover hit the Mars atmosphere at about 19,500 km/h and landed in Jezero Crater on its own. Its 'we've landed' signal took about 11.5 minutes to reach Earth.

c2_tagline.en: June 2018 · The storm that silenced Opportunity

c3_tagline.en: Sept 2017 · An X8.2 flare and an 11-minute delay

c4_tagline.en: May 2024 · Kerem is outside when the warning comes

c5_tagline.en: Real NASA DONKI data · updated daily

all_open.en: All chapters are open. Recommended: play them in order.

fail_air.en: The air ran out. In a dust storm, Life Support must come first.

fail_food.en: The food ran out. The greenhouse needed more.

fail_dose.en: The crew got too much radiation. Shelters and shields protect them.

g_tau.en: Tau tells how much dust blocks the Sun. On a clear Mars day it is about 0.5. Above 2, solar panels struggle. In June 2018 it reached 10.8.

g_sep.en: After a big flare, the Sun can throw out a storm of fast particles. Mars has a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field, so more of them reach the ground.

g_msv.en: mSv (millisievert) measures how much radiation a body takes in. NASA keeps an astronaut's whole career under 600 mSv.

g_flare.en: A sudden flash of energy on the Sun. Flares are ranked C, M and X; X is the strongest. An X8.2 is a very big one.

g_aurora.en: Glowing lights in the sky made when solar particles hit the air. On Earth they stay near the poles; on Mars they can cover the whole planet.

delay_title.en: Message from Earth on its way

delay_sub.en: Real Earth–Mars light delay today: {min} min. In the game, 1 minute = 1 second.

c2_sub.en: June 2018 · The storm that covered Mars

c2_l1.en: Commander, look at the horizon. The sky is getting darker every hour.

c2_l2.en: I measured the dust. [[Tau|tau]] jumped from 0.5 to over 3 in just a few days. That is exactly what NASA's Opportunity rover saw in June 2018.

c2_l3.en: This is a planet-wide storm. Our solar panels will make less and less power. We must decide fast.

c2_q1.en: The dust wall is here! Fold the solar panels?

c2_fold_h.en: Only 4 power during the storm, but the panels stay clean for later.

c2_leave_h.en: 6 power now, but dust sticks and the panels stay weaker forever.

c2_timeout.en: No order came... the panels are half covered. 5 power.

c2_w1.en: Storm mode! There isn't enough power for every room. Air comes first: give Life Support at least 2.

c2_r1.en: Tau is 6 now. The panels are barely working. We need to save something.

c2_r2.en: Tau 10.8! This is the darkest it got for Opportunity. It needed tau below 2 to recharge.

c2_r3.en: Still dark, but I think the dust is starting to settle. One more night.

c2_o_lab_h.en: Science stops, but that power keeps the air flowing.

c2_o_lights_h.en: Plants grow slower, but we save power for air.

c2_o_keep_h.en: Nothing stops... but the batteries drain fast.

c2_o_huddle_h.en: Heat and air only for one room. Less work gets done.

c2_o_eva.en: Send Deniz to brush the panels

c2_o_eva_h.en: A little more power, but walking in a dust storm is dangerous.

c2_o_snacks_h.en: Keeps the crew going, but the food reserve gets small.

c2_o_battery_h.en: Plenty of air tonight. The battery will be empty for the next storm.

c2_o_minimal_h.en: Lights off, lab off, greenhouse off. Cold and dark, but safe air.

c2_o_msg_h.en: Costs a little power. Earth will hear you in {min} minutes.

c2_eva_line.en: It's like walking inside a brown cloud. Panels brushed... coming back!

c2_clear1.en: Look! Sunlight! Tau is under 2 again. The panels are waking up.

c2_clear2.en: We made it. Opportunity was not so lucky. It went silent on June 10, 2018. NASA sent more than a thousand commands for eight months, and on February 13, 2019, they said goodbye.

c2_clear3.en: It was built for 90 sols and lasted almost 15 years. It drove more than 45 kilometres.

c2_s3.en: No one walked in the storm

c2_real.en: From late May to June 2018, a dust storm grew until it covered all of Mars. Opportunity measured tau 10.8 and lost power. Its last signal came on June 10, 2018.

c3_sub.en: September 2017 · A message that travels at the speed of light

c3_l1.en: Quiet night. My dose meter says we get about 0.64 [[mSv|msv]] every sol here. Curiosity measured that.

c3_l2.en: That's more than on Earth, because Mars has a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field to protect us.

c3_l3.en: Commander! Earth is sending us an urgent message. But it has to cross space first.

c3_prep.en: While we wait, how do we get ready?

c3_p_shield_h.en: Moves power from the lab to the shield.

c3_p_shelter_h.en: If we must hide, we will have food and water there.

c3_p_work_h.en: It might be nothing. More science for now.

c3_msg.en: Mission Control: "An X8.2 [[flare|flare]] just exploded on the Sun! A [[particle storm|sep]] may hit Mars. Take care!"

c3_late.en: Notice something? Earth saw the flare first, but their warning needed {min} minutes to reach us. Out here, we can't wait for Earth.

c3_alarm.en: RADIATION ALARM! Particles are hitting the base!

c3_shelter_h.en: Thick rock and water walls stop most particles. Work stops.

c3_stay_h.en: Science keeps going, but the crew takes the full dose.

c3_in1.en: We're in the lava tube. Rock above us, water tanks around us. The dose meter has calmed down.

c3_in2.en: A NASA scientist said it best: if you knew an event like this was coming during a Mars walk, you would definitely want to take shelter.

c3_out1.en: My meter is clicking like crazy... we got a big dose today.

c3_aurora1.en: Wait... come outside and look up! The whole sky is glowing green!

c3_aurora2.en: The same particles made an [[aurora|aurora]]. In September 2017, NASA's MAVEN saw one more than 25 times brighter than any before, and Curiosity measured radiation over twice as high as ever.

c3_s2.en: Went to the shelter in time

c3_real.en: On September 10–11, 2017, a big eruption on the Sun sent particles to Mars. Curiosity's RAD measured surface radiation more than twice as high as ever, for more than two days, and MAVEN saw a global aurora.

c4_l1.en: I found a rock with layers in it near the crater rim. It could hold clues about the old lake! I'm going out to get it.

c4_l2.en: Be careful, Kerem. Earth says sunspot region AR 3664 is very active this month. It gave Earth its strongest storm in 20 years.

c4_l3.en: I'm at the rock. It's beautiful! About 10 minutes to cut a sample.

c4_msg.en: Mission Control: "A huge flare, about X12, on the far side of the Sun. It's pointing at Mars. Particles may already be on the way!"

c4_q.en: Kerem is outside with no walls around him. Decide now!

c4_back_h.en: He leaves the rock behind. Safe, but we lose the sample.

c4_finish_h.en: 10 more minutes outside for a great discovery... and a big dose.

c4_rover.en: Send the rover for the rock

c4_rover_h.en: Kerem runs back; the rover fetches the rock but uses a lot of power.

c4_timeout.en: Kerem didn't hear an order and kept working!

c4_r_back.en: I'm running! ... I'm inside. My heart is racing, but I'm okay.

c4_r_finish.en: Got it! ... but my dose meter is screaming. Coming in now.

c4_r_rover.en: The rover has the rock! Kerem is safe. The batteries are low tonight.

c4_in1.en: Everybody in the lava tube, now!

c4_in2.en: Curiosity measured this storm on May 20, 2024: 8,100 micrograys. That's like 30 chest X-rays at once, the biggest it ever saw. Out in the open, that's a lot.

c4_in3.en: NASA says cliffs and lava tubes like ours give astronauts extra shielding. Good thing we built the shelter here.

c4_end1.en: No science result is worth the crew's health. Remember that, Commander.

c4_real.en: On May 20, 2024, a flare later estimated as X12 sent particles to Mars. Curiosity's RAD measured 8,100 micrograys, about 30 chest X-rays, the largest surge since it landed. MAVEN saw auroras across the planet.

c5_l1.en: This mission is different. I just downloaded REAL data from NASA's DONKI space-weather database: everything the Sun did in the last 30 days.

c5_l2.en: DONKI counts: {flr} flares, {cme} CMEs, {sep} particle storms, {gst} geomagnetic storms. Snapshot from {date}, updated once a day.

c5_calm.en: The real Sun was calm this month. No big particle storms. A perfect time for science, but calm days are when you prepare for the next storm.

c5_x_FLR.en: Flares are flashes of light. The danger is the particles that may follow.

c5_x_SEP.en: This is the dangerous kind. What do we do?

c5_x_CME.en: A cloud of solar gas. If it reaches Mars, we may see an aurora.

c5_x_GST.en: That one hit Earth, not us. Mars has no global magnetic field to make a storm like that.

c5_wake.en: Now share today's power for the base. Full sun: 10 ⚡.

c5_end.en: You just survived the Sun as it REALLY behaved this month. NASA mission planners check this same DONKI data every day. Come back tomorrow: the Sun will be different.

c5_s2.en: Kept the crew safe from every real event

c5_real.en: Every event in this chapter came from NASA's DONKI database (snapshot {date}). DONKI is run by the Community Coordinated Modeling Center at NASA Goddard.

c5_next.en: You finished the campaign! Replay any chapter to get 3 stars.

who_sub.en: Every astronaut keeps their own progress on this device.

grow_src.en: Real lettuce on the Space Station grew in 33–56 days (NASA OSDR · OSD-268). We fast-forward 33 days.

c5_l2v.en: Here is what NASA's DONKI recorded around the Sun in the last thirty days. The snapshot is updated once a day.

c5_ev_intro.en: Look at this real record from DONKI.

mg_valve_v.en: The oxygen maker is starting! Keep the pressure needle in the green zone.

mg_plants_v.en: Our plants need you! Tap the water drops and the light bulbs before they fade.

mg_fold_v.en: The dust wall is coming! Fold every solar panel, quick!

mg_dish_v.en: Turn the dish until you find Earth, and hold the signal steady.

mg_shelter_v.en: Particles are coming! Send everyone into the shelter, now!

mg_rover_v.en: Drive back to base! Jump over the rocks!

mm_i1.en: Welcome to Mars, Commander! Our job: survive ten sols, send science to Earth, and keep radiation low.

mm_i2.en: Three things keep us alive: oxygen, power, and protection from radiation. You can never max out all three. Tap any meter to learn why.

c1_trek.en: This is Jezero Crater, a real place: an old lake with a river delta. You can fly over it yourself in NASA Mars Trek.

why_moxie.en: Why can we breathe? Our oxygen maker works like MOXIE on Perseverance. MOXIE made real oxygen from Mars air: 122 grams in total.

why_rad.en: Even inside the base, space radiation reaches us: about 0.64 millisieverts every sol. Curiosity measures it every day.

why_tau.en: On a normal day, the dust number in the sky is about 0.5. In 2018 it reached 10.8, and Opportunity's panels went dark.

why_spirit.en: Wind can help too. In 2009 a gust cleaned Spirit's solar panels, and its power jumped.

why_ochmo.en: Hiding in the shelter cuts a solar storm's dose about in half. Against cosmic rays it helps only a little.

why_sep17.en: This really happened. In September 2017 a solar storm doubled the radiation on the surface of Mars.

c4_cmp_v.en: How big was our dose? Let's compare it with real numbers.

c4_cmp1.en: Curiosity measures about 6.4 millisieverts every ten sols, from cosmic rays alone.

c4_cmp2.en: On the Space Station, crews get about 80 to 160 millisieverts in six months. NASA's RadLab shows the real readings.

c4_cmp3.en: NASA's limit for a whole astronaut career is 600 millisieverts. That's why every shelter run matters.

c5_job_v.en: The Sun has had its say. Now choose the crew's job for today.

job_eva.en: Rocks tell the story of Mars. But outside there are no walls, so a solar storm hits you directly.

job_gym.en: Good choice. In space, bones can lose 1 to 1.5 percent of their strength every month without exercise.

job_plants.en: Plants are science and food. NASA grew radishes on the Space Station in just 27 days.

job_fix.en: Machines checked. On Mars, a broken oxygen maker is the biggest danger of all.

c5_src_live.en: This data came from NASA just now.
